ledger.note: 8 May 1860: Mosquera declares the Sovereign State of Cauca a separate nation. 'On May 8, 1860, the newly appointed Supreme Director of War Mosquera declared the Sovereign State of Cauca a separate nation'; the Granadine Confederation page dates the break by 'a decree of May 8, 1860'. Confidence 2 (reviewer am-08-g): the page names the Sovereign State of Cauca but not its extent; the three modern departments are a reading, and the war page's infobox puts Pasto (in Nariño) on the Confederation's side.

ledger.note: 1861: Santander, Boyacá, Magdalena and Tolima stand with Mosquera. The war page's infobox lists them on the rebel side without dates (page silent); Mosquera created Tolima out of Cundinamarca on 12 July 1861 (Granadine Confederation page). Year bridged from the Bogotá campaign, confidence 1.

ledger.note: 18 July 1861: Bogotá falls and the rebels become the government. 'the capital Bogotá fell to them on July 18, 1861' (the Granadine Confederation page gives 18 June 1861; the United States of Colombia page 'July 1861'). Mosquera, provisional president, governs the same state; the fighting against the Conservative holdouts (Antioquia, Pasto) goes on to November 1862.

Antioquia, 'a successful invasion of the region of Antioquia by the rebel army', where Braulio Henao resisted

wars.outcome: The rebels win: Bogotá falls on 18 July 1861, Mosquera becomes provisional president, and the war ends in November 1862 when the last Conservative leaders die or give up (the page also names 8 May 1863, the Rionegro Convention, as the formal end).
wars.note: Dates differ: Bogotá fell 18 July 1861 (war page) or 18 June 1861 (Granadine Confederation page); the war ends November 1862 (lead) or 8 May 1863 (body).

certainty.note: No frontier of the rebel states is given on any page; the modern departments are an approximation of states that were themselves loosely bounded.

notes: Rebel state that Cliopatria lacks: it held Cauca from 8 May 1860 and the other rebel states for part of the 14 months to the fall of Bogotá (18 July 1861), so it takes a type rebel dossier (brief section 6). Written from three pages, all opened for the Granadine Confederation dossier. Not settled: when Santander, Boyacá, Magdalena and Tolima came over (undated on the pages); the capital (page silent; Popayán is the researcher's reading); the date of Bogotá's fall (18 June or 18 July 1861); whether Panamá or Bolívar sided with either party (the infobox puts Panamá on the Confederation's side). The war continues after July 1861 against the Conservative holdouts in Antioquia and Pasto; it is in the Granadine Confederation's wars entry, not drawn as a rebel state.
